strengths: Introduces a well-motivated new task (interaction-aware RVOS) addressing a genuine gap in existing RVOS benchmarks, which largely treat referred objects in isolation without modeling actor-target relationships.

InterRVOS-8K is large in scale (127K expressions, 8.7K videos) with a high object-per-video ratio and explicit actor-target pair annotations, filling a niche not covered by prior datasets such as MeViS, ReVOS, or Ref-SAV.

The four-stage automated annotation pipeline (object description -> single/multi referring expressions -> interaction detection -> interaction-aware expression generation) is clearly described and the prompts are provided in the appendix, aiding transparency.

ReVIOSa's actor/target special-token design ([SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR]) is a reasonable and simple extension to existing SAM2+MLLM segmentation frameworks, and the paper provides an ablation (Table 6) showing the benefit of joint versus independent token supervision.

Experiments span multiple axes: cross-dataset training comparisons (Ref-SAV vs InterRVOS subsets), per-caption-type breakdowns, zero-shot generalization to MeViS/Ref-YoutubeVOS/Ref-DAVIS, and qualitative examples, providing a fairly comprehensive empirical picture.
The proposed actor-target-aware evaluation protocol is a useful complementary metric for probing interaction understanding specifically, beyond aggregate J&F scores.
weaknesses: The dataset's core value rests entirely on automatically generated (GPT-4o/LLaMA-70B) captions and interaction/role labels, yet the paper reports no human verification, annotator agreement, or quality/error-rate analysis of the pipeline's outputs (e.g., correctness of unidirectional vs bidirectional classification, actor/target role assignment accuracy). This is a significant gap given that the entire contribution hinges on data quality.

The evaluation set itself is constructed via the same automatic pipeline (with filtering to boost interaction-centric samples), so any systematic errors or biases in caption/mask generation likely propagate into the benchmark used to score all models, undermining the reliability of reported comparisons.

It is not clearly explained how pixel-level segmentation masks are derived from VidOR (which provides bounding boxes, not masks) — this critical annotation detail for ground-truth mask tracks is missing or unclear.

Baseline comparisons are relatively narrow: the main quantitative comparison is against Sa2VA (upon which ReVIOSa is directly built), Referformer, and LMPM; more recent MLLM-based segmentation methods cited in the related work (e.g., VideoGLaMM, VISA, ViLLa) are not benchmarked, making it harder to assess how much of the gain is attributable to the proposed architecture versus the underlying MLLM+SAM2 backbone.

The architectural novelty is incremental — extending a single [SEG] token to a pair of [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens is a fairly straightforward modification of existing LISA/Sa2VA-style token-prompted segmentation, rather than a substantially new modeling approach for relational reasoning.

The video clip extraction procedure (selecting only first/last 1000-frame bins and truncating to 500 frames) appears somewhat arbitrary and could bias the dataset toward specific temporal segments of long videos, potentially limiting temporal diversity.

Performance on interaction expressions specifically is noted to be lower than other categories (Table 4), and while attributed to the need for architecture improvements, this is not deeply analyzed with error cases or ablations isolating why interaction reasoning remains harder.

The paper's actor-target-aware evaluation depends on expressions where the correct actor/target split is unambiguous, but for interactions involving 3+ objects (noted as 20.3% of interactions), the actor-target framing may be an oversimplification, and this complexity is not thoroughly discussed or evaluated.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and underexplored gap in RVOS — modeling actor-target interaction roles rather than single isolated referents — which is a reasonable and useful task formulation.

Proposes a scalable, automated multi-stage annotation pipeline (GPT-4o + LLaMA-70B) that produces a dataset with substantially more expressions (127K) and higher object-per-video density than prior RVOS datasets, potentially useful as a resource.
Introduces a simple extension to MLLM+SAM2 architectures ([SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens) that is easy to understand and integrate into existing segmentation-token-based pipelines.

Provides a reasonably broad set of experiments: comparison to multiple baselines (ReferFormer, LMPM, Sa2VA), ablations on token design, zero-shot transfer experiments to MeViS/Ref-YouTube-VOS/Ref-DAVIS, and caption-type breakdowns.
Numerous qualitative examples and dataset statistics (word frequency, interaction counts, object counts) are provided for transparency.
weaknesses: The dataset is entirely automatically annotated (captions, interaction detection, actor/target role assignment, merge decisions) using GPT-4o and a quantized LLaMA-70B, yet no human verification, inter-annotator agreement, or quality/error-rate analysis is reported anywhere in the main paper or appendix. Given that LLMs are known to hallucinate relationships and misassign actor/target roles, this is a critical gap for a paper whose central contribution is a benchmark dataset — the trustworthiness of the ground-truth labels (including the evaluation set) is unverified.

It is unclear how pixel-level segmentation masks were obtained for InterRVOS-8K. VidOR natively provides bounding-box trajectories, not pixel masks; the paper does not explain the process used to convert these into the segmentation masks used for training/evaluation (e.g., whether SAM2 or another automatic segmenter was used, and with what accuracy). This is a significant methodological omission that affects reproducibility and correctness of the reported J&F metrics.

The evaluation set is constructed from the same VidOR training split (just disjoint videos) and filtered to increase interaction-centric samples, so it is not an independent, out-of-domain benchmark; claims of generalization are therefore weaker than implied, and the "zero-shot" results on MeViS/Ref-DAVIS are the only real out-of-domain evidence, with comparatively modest gains.

The architecture as presented (a single actor–single target pair of tokens) does not obviously handle the multi-object actor/target cases shown in the dataset examples (e.g., "Actor [2] / Target [0], [1]"), yet no architectural explanation or ablation addresses how multiple targets per actor are segmented with only two special tokens — this is a mismatch between the claimed dataset diversity and the model's capability.

Reported performance improvements over the strongest baseline (Sa2VA-4B) are modest overall (J&F 60.0 vs 58.5 overall; 56.4 vs 55.3 on Referring), and the 1B variant occasionally outperforms the 4B variant, which is not discussed or explained, raising questions about the robustness/significance of the gains given no variance/multiple-run reporting.

Comparisons against ReferFormer and LMPM use much older, non-MLLM, significantly smaller-capacity architectures, making the headline "state-of-the-art" claims somewhat uneven; a more controlled comparison (e.g., retraining comparable-capacity baselines on the same data) would strengthen the claims.

The paper's claim of being the "largest" dataset rests on counting automatically generated expression variants (appearance-only/motion-only/combined/class-level/appearance-level paraphrases of the same underlying interaction) rather than independently annotated referring instances, which somewhat inflates the apparent scale relative to manually annotated datasets like MeViS or ReVOS.

Performance on the paper's own "Interaction" caption category is consistently among the lowest across experiments (e.g., Table 4), suggesting the core contribution (interaction understanding) remains the weakest point even with the proposed data and architecture, which undercuts the paper's central claims of effectively solving interaction-aware segmentation.
Presentation issues: some grammatical errors ("a actor-target joint segmentation framework", "models decide"), and limited analysis of failure cases or dataset annotation noise in the main text.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and underexplored gap in RVOS literature: existing datasets/models treat referred objects in isolation and rarely model directional actor-target relationships, motivating a well-justified new task formulation.

InterRVOS-8K is large in scale (127K expressions, 8.7K videos, 17.6K annotated interactions) and is the first RVOS dataset to explicitly separate actor and target roles with paired complementary expressions, which is a useful resource contribution.

The four-stage automated annotation pipeline (single-object captioning, single/multi-instance expression generation, interaction detection, and role-aware expression synthesis) is clearly described and includes concrete example outputs and full prompt listings in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.

The proposed actor-target-aware evaluation protocol is a sensible complement to standard J&F metrics, enabling more targeted assessment of interaction understanding rather than only aggregate accuracy.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: comparisons against Ref-SAV/MeViS training data at controlled sample sizes, caption-type breakdowns, zero-shot transfer to MeViS/Ref-YouTube-VOS/Ref-DAVIS, and architecture ablations (single token vs. independent vs. joint actor/target tokens) that support the core claims.

ReVIOSa achieves consistent improvements over strong recent baselines (Sa2VA-1B/4B, Referformer, LMPM) across Referring, Actor-Target, and Overall settings, and notably the 1B variant surpasses the 4B baseline, suggesting the architectural change (or data) is contributing beyond scale alone.
weaknesses: The entire dataset (including the evaluation/test split) is generated and filtered by GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B without any reported human verification, inter-annotator agreement, or manual quality audit; since the benchmark's ground-truth interaction labels and directionality (who is actor vs. target) are themselves model-generated, errors or hallucinated relationships could propagate silently into both training supervision and evaluation, undermining confidence in reported numbers.

There is a degree of circularity in benchmarking: the InterRVOS-8K eval set is constructed by the same automatic pipeline as the training data, so strong performance on this benchmark may partly reflect distributional match to pipeline artifacts/biases rather than genuine interaction understanding; independent human-annotated test cases would strengthen the claim.

The architectural contribution is relatively incremental — essentially adding a second special segmentation token ([SEG_TAR]) alongside the existing [SEG_ACT]/[SEG] mechanism used in prior MLLM+SAM2 pipelines (e.g., Sa2VA) — rather than a new mechanism for reasoning about relations between the two tokens (e.g., no explicit relational/graph module beyond joint token co-training).

The video clip extraction procedure (only first and last 1000-frame bins, keeping only the first 500 frames of each) is somewhat arbitrary and could bias which portions of long videos are sampled, potentially limiting the diversity of interactions actually captured despite the claimed scale.

The model handles only unidirectional interactions with the dual-token mechanism; bidirectional interactions collapse to a single [SEG_ACT] output, so the architecture does not fully exploit the bidirectional interaction annotations present in the dataset, leaving part of the proposed task under-modeled.

Baseline comparisons in the main table are limited to a small set of methods (Referformer, LMPM, Sa2VA); other more recent MLLM-based segmentation methods mentioned in related work (e.g., VideoGLaMM, VISA, LLaVA-based approaches with special tokens) are not directly compared, limiting the strength of the state-of-the-art claim.

Performance on the 'Interaction' caption category is reported as slightly lower than other categories even with the proposed dataset (Table 4), and the paper does not deeply analyze failure modes or provide error analysis for why interaction expressions remain comparatively harder, which would help substantiate the practical usefulness of the approach.

Source videos are drawn solely from VidOR, which centers on everyday human/animal interactions; generalization of the interaction-centric supervision to other domains (e.g., sports, industrial, egocentric video) is not evaluated, so the breadth of applicability of the dataset and model design remains untested.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and novel task extension to RVOS: explicit actor-target role separation for interaction expressions, which addresses a genuine gap in existing RVOS literature that treats interactions as single-object or grouped-motion segmentation.

Contributes a large-scale automatically annotated dataset (InterRVOS-127K, 127K expressions, 8.7K videos) that is substantially larger than prior datasets and uniquely provides actor-target mask pairs; the four-stage annotation pipeline (object description, expression generation, interaction detection with directionality, and role-aware expression synthesis) is clearly described and includes human refinement of the evaluation set.

Proposes a reasonably simple and effective architectural extension (dual [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens plus attention mask loss) that is compatible with existing MLLM+SAM2 pipelines, with ablations showing complementary contributions of each component (+2.6 for tokens, +1.5 for AML, +5.0 combined).

Extensive supporting analysis in the appendix, including layer-head selection rationale for AML, attention correlation studies motivating the loss, qualitative visualizations, and zero-shot/cross-dataset comparisons showing InterRVOS-127K provides good data efficiency and transfer versus Ref-SAV/ReVOS.

Reasonable performance gains are shown not only on the new InterRVOS-Actor/Target split but also on standard RVOS benchmarks (MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, Ref-DAVIS), suggesting the approach is not narrowly overfit to the new benchmark.
weaknesses: The dataset is fully automatically generated using GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B captioning plus SAM2 mask tracks, with only the evaluation set receiving human correction; there is no reported quality metric (e.g., human agreement, annotation error rate) for the training set or a rigorous quantification of the evaluation-set correction process, raising quality concerns for a dataset contribution positioned as a primary contribution.

Baseline comparisons for the new InterRVOS-Target setting are essentially only against the paper's own model variants, since prior methods are described as inherently incapable of producing a target mask; this makes the 'state-of-the-art' claim for interaction-aware segmentation somewhat vacuous without a naive baseline (e.g., prompting existing models twice with actor-focused and target-focused phrasings) to isolate the true benefit of the proposed architecture.

The evaluation protocol details (e.g., how ground-truth actor/target roles are matched to model outputs, how errors in the model's own interaction-vs-non-interaction decision affect scoring) are not fully specified in the main text, which could materially affect interpretation of the reported J&F improvements.

The architectural novelty is somewhat incremental (token duplication plus an attention-supervision auxiliary loss), and the paper does not compare against a simpler baseline isolating whether gains stem from additional supervision signal (more masks/loss terms) versus a qualitatively different interaction understanding.

It is unclear how multi-object interactions (up to 20.3% involve three objects per the dataset statistics) are handled within the binary actor/target framework used for both annotation and evaluation.

Presentation is dense with heavy reliance on the appendix for essential experimental details (e.g., standard RVOS benchmark comparisons, zero-shot results, prompt templates), somewhat undermining the self-containedness of the main paper.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and underexplored gap in RVOS: existing benchmarks and models collapse multi-object interactions into a single referred 'actor', ignoring the target object's role, and the paper's task formulation (separate actor/target masks with directionality) is a reasonable and useful extension.

Produces a large-scale, automatically annotated dataset (127K expressions) that is the first to our knowledge to include explicit actor/target mask pairs for interactions, which could be a useful resource if annotation quality is trustworthy.

The attention analysis (Figure 6, A1-A5) showing correlation between attention concentration on GT mask regions and segmentation quality, and the layer/head selection study, is a reasonably careful empirical investigation that at least partially justifies the design of the auxiliary loss.

Qualitative examples convincingly illustrate that the baseline (Sa2VA) collapses actor/target distinctions while the proposed special-token mechanism produces separated masks for simple interaction phrases.
Extensive appendix with ablations, zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation, and dataset statistics gives some transparency into the data composition and model behavior.
weaknesses: The entire 127K training set (minus the 738 held-out videos) is annotated automatically by GPT-4o/LLaMA-70B with no reported human verification of quality, correctness, or actor/target role accuracy; there is no quantitative measure (e.g., human agreement, precision of role-assignment, caption-mask alignment) to support the reliability of this large corpus, which undermines confidence in both training supervision and claims about 'high-quality' annotation.

It is not made clear in the main text whether baseline methods (ReferFormer, LMPM, VISA, VideoLISA, Sa2VA) in Table 2 are fine-tuned on the same InterRVOS-127K training data as ReVIOSa or evaluated zero-shot/off-the-shelf; this materially affects whether the comparison is fair, and the ambiguity is a significant weakness for the central quantitative claim of state-of-the-art performance.

The core architectural contribution—replacing a single [SEG] token with two role-specific tokens [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR]—is an incremental extension of existing [SEG]-token MLLM segmentation frameworks (LISA, VISA, Sa2VA) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the novelty largely resides in the task/data framing rather than the model.

The attention mask loss (AML) layer-head selection procedure is a brittle, two-stage, model-specific heuristic (train once, inspect attention magnitudes, manually pick top-1 layer and top-4 heads) that must be re-derived for every backbone/scale, which limits generality, reproducibility, and practical applicability; the paper does not discuss how sensitive results are to this selection or whether it generalizes to unseen domains.

Since no existing baseline can be evaluated on the InterRVOS-Target split (by design), the reported 'state-of-the-art' target-segmentation numbers for ReVIOSa are not benchmarked against any competing approach, so the task's claimed difficulty/discriminative power is validated only internally (via ablations) rather than against the field.

The dataset is derived solely from VidOR videos, which skews toward specific interaction types (mostly human-human/human-object with VidOR's object vocabulary); no analysis is given on how well the task/dataset generalizes to interactions outside this distribution, and the 'top-2 object' interaction assumption (~80% of interactions involve exactly 2 objects per Fig. A8h) suggests limited structural complexity despite claims of fine-grained relational modeling.

Related concepts (actor-predicate-target triplets, scene graphs, HOI datasets such as Action Genome/VidOR/VidVRD) are discussed but the paper does not empirically compare against or build on these richer relational vocabularies (predicates), reducing the work's conceptual contribution to merely binary actor/target segmentation without the predicate semantics that define the interaction itself.

Performance gains from the proposed AML are modest (+1.5 J&F in isolation) relative to the gain from merely adding two decoupled tokens (+2.6), raising a question of whether AML's added complexity (custom supervision, head/layer search) is justified by its practical benefit.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and novel task (InterRVOS) that identifies a genuine gap in standard RVOS: most existing methods collapse interaction expressions into a single referred object, ignoring the asymmetric actor/target roles that are semantically central to describing many video events.

Proposes a large-scale (127K expression) automatically annotated dataset with a carefully designed four-stage pipeline (object appearance/motion extraction, single/multi-instance expression generation, interaction detection with directionality, and interaction-aware expression generation) that is clearly documented with prompts and examples in the appendix.

The architectural contribution (dual [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens plus attention mask loss) is simple, technically sound, and well-motivated by an empirical analysis showing correlation between attention concentration on object regions and segmentation quality (Appendix B.1).

Extensive ablations and analyses: layer/head selection study for AML, supervised vs. non-supervised head comparisons, per-component ablation (Table 4), and zero-shot generalization experiments across multiple standard RVOS benchmarks (Appendix C.2-C.3), lending good support to the claims.

Strong empirical results: ReVIOSa outperforms strong existing MLLM-based baselines (Sa2VA, VideoLISA, VISA) on both interaction-aware and standard RVOS settings despite comparable or smaller model sizes, and the dataset itself is shown to be more sample-efficient than a comparable automatically-annotated dataset (Ref-SAV).
Good presentation: clear figures illustrating the task, pipeline, architecture, and attention visualizations aid understanding and reproducibility of the core ideas.
weaknesses: Because the dataset is fully automatically annotated (GPT-4o + LLaMA-70B) except for the manually refined evaluation set, the paper provides no quantitative measure of annotation quality/accuracy for the training data (e.g., human audit of actor/target role correctness, interaction directionality accuracy, or caption faithfulness), leaving open the possibility of systematic labeling noise that is hard to detect from downstream metrics alone.

In Table 2, the InterRVOS-Target column can only be compared against the paper's own two model variants (ReVIOSa-1B/4B) since no baseline supports target segmentation; this makes the 'state-of-the-art' claim on InterRVOS-Target somewhat vacuous as a comparison, since there is no independent point of reference for what a reasonable target-segmentation score should be.

The layer-head selection strategy for AML (top-1 layer, top-4 heads) is derived empirically per model without a principled justification for why this specific configuration generalizes, and the paper does not discuss sensitivity/robustness of this choice across different backbones or training runs beyond the 1B/4B cases shown.

The video clip extraction procedure (only first and last 500-frame bins of long source videos) is an ad hoc heuristic that could bias the dataset toward particular scene types or interaction moments, and its effect on dataset diversity/quality is not analyzed.

Some standard-RVOS benchmark comparisons mix models of different scales and base LLMs (e.g., 7B/13B vs. the proposed 1B/4B), which somewhat complicates fair attribution of gains to the proposed method versus base model capacity, though the paper does partially address this by noting ReVIOSa's smaller size.
